title: Give him bread (Proverbs 25:21)
hookLine: "If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat"
carry: the need comes first, and the history comes second

cards: Someone knocks just as the bread comes out of the oven. Handing a slice to a friend would take no thought at all. Now change one thing.
The person standing at the door, hungry, is someone you'd rather not see: the neighbor who complained about you, the coworker who took the credit, someone who once wished you harm and said so.
Does the bread still get handed over? Proverbs answers in one plain sentence.

teach.b: In the King James words: "If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink." No other conditions. Not if he apologizes, not if he's earned it.

teach.h: IF THINE ENEMY BE HUNGRY, GIVE HIM BREAD.
teach.b: If he's hungry. The need comes first, and the history comes second. The verse goes on with a strange picture: for thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head, and the LORD shall reward thee.
Readers differ on the coals. Some hear the burning shame of being treated kindly by someone you wronged, a shame that might turn into regret. Others hear warmth, a kindness that melts the hostility.
The picture stays open. The Torah already says something close.
In Exodus, if you find your enemy's ox or donkey wandering, you bring it back, and if the donkey of someone who hates you is lying under its load, you help lift it.
The rule doesn't ask you to like the person, only to help with the animal.

In Kings, an army from Aram comes after the prophet Elisha and is struck so it can't see where it's going. Elisha leads the soldiers into Samaria, into the hands of the king of Israel, who asks, shall I strike them?

No, says Elisha: set bread and water before them, and send them home. The king prepares a great meal, and they eat, drink and go home to their master. And the raiding bands of Aram came no more into the land of Israel.
The very next verse brings a full war, so the peace isn't forever. But the raids ended at a table, not at sword point.

how: Jewish teaching links Proverbs 25:21 with the Torah's commands to help an enemy's stray or overloaded animal (Exodus 23:4–5), and the line is studied as part of how to treat people you're in conflict with.

s: Proverbs says to feed an enemy only if he apologizes
the verse has one condition: if he is hungry.
the Torah tells you to help your enemy's overloaded donkey
Exodus 23:5: you help, whatever you feel about its owner.
after Elisha's meal, the raiding bands of Aram came no more
2 Kings 6:23: the raids ended at a table, though war returns in the next verse.

games.q: you're the king of Israel. the enemy soldiers are helpless in your city. Elisha is standing beside you. what happens?
o: feed them and send them home.
games.why: Elisha says set bread and water before them. the king makes a great meal, and the raids stop.

practice: Bring to mind someone you'd usually walk the long way around to avoid, and picture them a little hungry, a little tired.

Picture handing them something small, a coffee, a snack, a share of what's on the table; you don't have to feel warm about it, just see your hand reaching out. If you pray, you can ask for an open hand.

wordCard.voice: Elisha, the prophet who set bread and water before a raiding army from Aram, then sent it home. Today's word.
